messages.content: Can you retrieve the weather forecast this coming Saturday?

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL to retrieve weather data from the Open-Meteo API. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: URL of the Open-Meteo API endpoint.

headers.description: Headers to include in the request. Each key-value pair represents a header field and its value.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

timeout.description: Maximum time in seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters for the GET request.

latitude.description: Latitude of the location, positive for N and negative for S. This is a float type value.

longitude.description: Longitude of the location, positive for E and negative for W. This is a float type value.

elevation.description: Elevation in meters above sea level for the location. The default value represents no elevation downscaling.

auth.description: Authentication tuple for HTTP authentication, in the format (username, password).

cert.description: Path to the SSL client certificate file (.pem). A null value means no client certificate is used.

cookies.description: Dictionary of cookies to send with the request. Each key represents a cookie name.

proxies.description: Dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy. Each key-value pair represents a protocol and its proxy URL.

stream.description: If True, the response should be streamed; otherwise, it should be downloaded immediately.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate.

message.content: Sure! To give you an accurate forecast for this coming Saturday (2026‑06‑12), I’ll need your location. Could you let me know the latitude and longitude of the place you’re interested in? If you prefer, just tell me the city or town name and I’ll look up the coordinates for you.
message.reasoning:
The user wants the weather forecast for this coming Saturday. We need to use the Open-Meteo API. We need to determine the date for "this coming Saturday". Today is 2026-06-06. Let's check what day of week that is. 2026-06-06 is a Thursday? Let's calculate: 2026-06-06. 2026 is not a leap year? 2026 is not divisible by 4, so not a leap year. 2026-01-01 was a Friday? Actually let's compute quickly: 2025-01-01 was a Wednesday? Wait, we can approximate: 2024-01-01 was a Monday (since 2024 is a leap year starting on Monday). 2025-01-01 would be Wednesday (since 2024 had 366 days, adding 2 days). 2026-01-01 would be Thursday (since 2025 had 365 days, adding 1 day). So 2026-01-01 is Thursday. Then 2026-06-06 is 31+28+31+30+31+6 days after Jan 1. Sum: Jan 31 days, Feb 28, Mar 31, Apr 30, May 31, plus 6 days in June. Total days after Jan 1: 31+28+31+30+31+6 = 157 days. 157 mod 7 = 157 - 7*22 = 157 - 154 = 3. So 2026-06-06 is Thursday + 3 days = Sunday? Wait, Jan 1 is Thursday. Add 157 days: 157 mod 7 = 3. So day of week = Thursday + 3 days = Sunday. So 2026-06-06 is a Sunday. That means "this coming Saturday" would be the next Saturday after today, which is 2026-06-11. Because 2026-06-07 is Monday, 2026-06-08 Tuesday, 2026-06-09 Wednesday, 2026-06-10 Thursday, 2026-06-11 Friday? Wait, let's list: 2026-06-06 Sunday. Next day 2026-06-07 Monday. 2026-06-08 Tuesday. 2026-06-09 Wednesday. 2026-06-10 Thursday. 2026-06-11 Friday. 2026-06-12 Saturday. So "this coming Saturday" is 2026-06-12. So we need forecast for 2026-06-12.

We need to call the Open-Meteo API. We need to specify latitude and longitude. But the user hasn't provided a location. We need to ask for location. Or we could assume a default location? The user didn't specify. We should ask for location. But maybe we can ask for the user's location. So we should ask: "Sure, could you provide your location (latitude and longitude)?" Alternatively, we could ask for city name. But the API requires lat/lon. So we ask for lat/lon. Or we could ask for city name and then geocode. But we don't have geocoding tool. So we ask for lat/lon. So we respond asking for location.
